+----------+---------+----------------------------------+

Hindi in UTF-8:
'न' = E0 A4 A8 (3 bytes)
'म' = E0 A4 AE (3 bytes)
'स' = E0 A4 B8 (3 bytes)

Without proper encoding: "à¤¨à¤®à¤¸à¥à¤¤à¥" (mojibake!)
hinglish_explanation: Yaar computers text ko numbers mein store karte hain. ASCII sirf English handle karta hai. UTF-8 duniya ki saari languages handle karta hai - Hindi, Tamil, Arabic sab. Agar encoding galat hai to 'नमस्ते' garbage characters ban jaata hai. NLP mein sahi encoding bahut zaroori hai.
real_life_example: Bahut baar Indian language datasets mein encoding issues aate hain - Hindi text CSV mein open karo to garbage dikhta hai kyunki UTF-8 mein save nahi hua. WhatsApp messages export karo to Hindi properly aati hai kyunki UTF-8 use hota hai.
how_to_answer: - Text encoding maps characters to numerical representations for computers
- ASCII: 128 characters, English only - insufficient for multilingual NLP
- Unicode: standard covering 150,000+ characters from all writing systems
- UTF-8: variable-length Unicode encoding, most common on web
- Critical for Indian language NLP: Devanagari, Tamil, Telugu need Unicode
- Common issues: mojibake (garbled text), mixed encodings in datasets
- Always specify encoding when reading files: open(file, encoding='utf-8')

question: What is the difference between syntax and semantics in NLP?
diagram:
Syntax (Structure/Grammar):
"The cat chased the mouse" -> Valid syntax ✓
"Cat the mouse chased the" -> Invalid syntax ✗

Semantics (Meaning):
"Colorless green ideas sleep furiously" -> Valid syntax ✓, No meaning ✗
"The cat chased the mouse" -> Valid syntax ✓, Meaningful ✓

NLP Processing:
+--------+     +----------+     +----------+
| Lexical| --> | Syntactic| --> | Semantic |
| (words)|     | (grammar)|     | (meaning)|
+--------+     +----------+     +----------+
hinglish_explanation: Bhai syntax matlab grammar rules - sentence structure sahi hai ya nahi. Semantics matlab meaning - sentence ka matlab kya hai. 'Rang birangi hari ideas gusse se soti hain' grammatically sahi hai par meaningless hai. NLP ko dono samajhna padta hai.
real_life_example: Grammarly syntax check karta hai - grammar galat hai to red underline. Google Search semantics samajhta hai - 'How to make chai' search karne pe chai recipe milti hai, exact words match nahi chahiye. Alexa India ko bhi syntax aur semantics dono process karne padte hain.
how_to_answer: - Syntax: rules governing sentence structure and word arrangement
- Semantics: meaning conveyed by words and sentences
- Syntactic analysis: POS tagging, parsing, grammar checking
- Semantic analysis: word sense disambiguation, sentiment, intent
- A sentence can be syntactically correct but semantically meaningless
- Pragmatics: meaning in context (sarcasm, implication) - beyond syntax and semantics
- Modern NLP models like BERT capture both syntactic and semantic patterns

question: What is the Naive Bayes classifier and why is it popular for text classification?
diagram:
Naive Bayes for Text:
P(class|document) ∝ P(class) * ∏ P(word_i|class)

Example - Spam Detection:
P(Spam|"free money click") ∝ P(Spam) * P(free|Spam) * P(money|Spam) * P(click|Spam)
                           = 0.4 * 0.8 * 0.7 * 0.6 = 0.1344

P(Ham|"free money click")  ∝ P(Ham) * P(free|Ham) * P(money|Ham) * P(click|Ham)
                           = 0.6 * 0.1 * 0.2 * 0.1 = 0.0012

Result: Spam (much higher probability)
hinglish_explanation: Yaar Naive Bayes ek simple probabilistic classifier hai. 'Naive' isliye kyunki ye assume karta hai ki saare words independent hain (jo sach nahi hai par kaam achha karta hai). Text classification mein popular hai kyunki fast hai, kam data pe bhi achha karta hai, aur surprisingly accurate hai.
real_life_example: Rediffmail ka spam filter Naive Bayes use karta tha - 'lottery', 'winner', 'click here' jaise words ki probability high thi spam mein. MoneyControl app news articles ko categories mein classify karne ke liye NB use karta hai. Simple aur effective hai.
how_to_answer: - Naive Bayes applies Bayes theorem with independence assumption between features
- Popular for text because: fast training, works with small data, scales well
- Variants: Multinomial NB (word counts), Bernoulli NB (binary), Gaussian NB
- Multinomial NB most common for text classification
- Naive assumption (word independence) rarely true but still works well
- Often used as baseline for text classification tasks
- Handles high-dimensional sparse data (text) efficiently

question: What is the difference between information retrieval (IR) and information extraction (IE)?
diagram:
Information Retrieval (IR):
Query: "best restaurants Mumbai"
Result: [Doc1, Doc2, Doc3, ...] (ranked documents)
-> Find relevant documents

Information Extraction (IE):
Input: "Taj Hotel Mumbai was rated 4.5 stars by 2000 users"
Output: {
  entity: "Taj Hotel",
  location: "Mumbai",
  rating: 4.5,
  num_reviews: 2000
}
-> Extract structured data from text
hinglish_explanation: Bhai IR matlab query deke relevant documents dhundho - jaise Google Search karta hai. IE matlab document se structured information nikalo - jaise resume se name, email, experience extract karo. IR documents return karta hai, IE data points return karta hai.
real_life_example: Google Search IR hai - tu query deta hai, relevant web pages milte hain. Naukri.com ka resume parser IE hai - resume upload karo, automatically name, skills, experience extract ho jaata hai structured form mein. Justdial bhi business listings se IE karta hai.
how_to_answer: - IR: finding relevant documents from a collection given a query
- IE: extracting structured information (entities, relations) from text
- IR returns documents, IE returns structured data
- IR techniques: TF-IDF, BM25, vector search, ranking algorithms
- IE techniques: NER, relation extraction, event extraction, template filling
- They complement each other: IR finds docs, IE extracts info from them
- Applications: IR for search engines, IE for knowledge base construction

question: What are word clouds and how are they generated from text?
diagram:
Input Text: Multiple Flipkart reviews about a phone

Word Cloud Output:
          camera
    battery    DISPLAY     good
  performance     FAST
      value    price    screen
    amazing   quality   best
        smooth    excellent

(Size of word ∝ frequency in text)

Steps: Text -> Preprocess -> Count frequencies -> Visualize
hinglish_explanation: Yaar word cloud ek visualization hai jismein frequently occurring words bade dikhte hain aur rare words chhote. Text preprocess karo, word frequencies count karo, phir visualize karo. Quick insight milta hai ki text mein kya important hai - EDA ke liye useful hai.
real_life_example: Flipkart product page pe review insights mein word cloud jaisi feature hoti hai - 'camera', 'battery', 'display' bade mein dikhte hain. Political analysis mein Modi ji ke speeches ka word cloud banao to 'vikas', 'India', 'development' prominent honge.
how_to_answer: - Word clouds visualize word frequency with size proportional to occurrence
- Steps: preprocess text, remove stop words, count frequencies, render
- Useful for quick EDA and presentation of text data
- Libraries: wordcloud (Python), can customize colors, shapes, fonts
- Limitations: no context, no sentiment, can be misleading
- Better alternatives for analysis: TF-IDF scores, topic models
- Good for stakeholder presentations, quick data understanding

question: What is Levenshtein distance (edit distance) and where is it used in NLP?
diagram:
Levenshtein Distance between "kitten" and "sitting":

kitten -> sitten (substitute k->s)    cost: 1
sitten -> sittin (substitute e->i)    cost: 1
sittin -> sitting (insert g)          cost: 1

Total Edit Distance = 3

Operations allowed:
- Insert a character (cost: 1)
- Delete a character (cost: 1)
- Replace a character (cost: 1)

DP Matrix:
    ""  s  i  t  t  i  n  g
"" [ 0  1  2  3  4  5  6  7]
k  [ 1  1  2  3  4  5  6  7]
i  [ 2  2  1  2  3  4  5  6]
t  [ 3  3  2  1  2  3  4  5]
...
hinglish_explanation: Bhai edit distance matlab ek string ko doosri string mein convert karne ke liye minimum kitne operations (insert/delete/replace) chahiye. 'Cat' ko 'Car' banana hai - sirf 't' ko 'r' se replace karo - distance = 1. Spell checking, fuzzy matching mein bahut use hota hai.
real_life_example: Flipkart search pe 'samung' type karo to 'Samsung' suggest karta hai kyunki edit distance kam hai. Ola app mein 'Connaght Place' type karo to 'Connaught Place' correct kar deta hai. Aadhaar verification mein name matching bhi edit distance se hoti hai approximate matching ke liye.
how_to_answer: - Levenshtein distance counts minimum edits (insert, delete, replace) between two strings
- Computed using dynamic programming in O(m*n) time and space
- Applications: spell correction, fuzzy string matching, DNA sequence alignment
- Variants: Damerau-Levenshtein (adds transposition), weighted edit distance
- Used in approximate string matching and record linkage/deduplication
- Normalized edit distance = edit_dist / max(len(s1), len(s2)) for comparison
- Libraries: python-Levenshtein, fuzzywuzzy/rapidfuzz for fuzzy matching

question: What are collocations in NLP and how do you detect them?
diagram:
Collocations: Words that co-occur more than by chance

Examples:
- "strong tea" (not "powerful tea")
- "heavy rain" (not "strong rain")  
- "New Delhi" (proper noun collocation)
- "machine learning" (technical collocation)

Detection Methods:
+------------------+----------------------------------+
| Frequency        | Count bigram occurrences         |
| PMI              | log2(P(x,y) / P(x)*P(y))       |
| Chi-squared      | Statistical significance test    |
| t-test           | Compare observed vs expected     |
+------------------+----------------------------------+
hinglish_explanation: Yaar collocations wo words hain jo naturally saath mein aate hain - 'strong coffee' bolte hain, 'powerful coffee' nahi. NLP mein ye detect karna important hai kyunki ye ek unit ki tarah kaam karte hain. PMI (Pointwise Mutual Information) se pata chalta hai ki do words chance se zyada saath aa rahe hain.
real_life_example: Google Trends India mein 'Lok Sabha elections' ek collocation hai - ye words saath mein aate hain. News articles mein 'Supreme Court', 'Prime Minister', 'stock market' collocations hain. Zomato reviews mein 'butter chicken', 'dal makhani' collocations hain jo dishes identify karti hain.
how_to_answer: - Collocations are word combinations that occur together more than by chance
- Types: fixed phrases, proper nouns, technical terms, idiomatic expressions
- PMI measures how much more likely words co-occur vs independently
- Chi-squared and t-test provide statistical significance of co-occurrence
- Important for: phrase detection, machine translation, information extraction
- NLTK provides BigramCollocationFinder and TrigramCollocationFinder
- Used in keyphrase extraction and multi-word expression detection

question: What is keyword extraction and what methods are used?
diagram:
Document: "Machine learning algorithms improve NLP tasks..."

Keyword Extraction Methods:
+------------------+-----------------------------------+
| TF-IDF           | High TF-IDF score words           |
| RAKE             | Rapid Automatic Keyword Extract   |
| TextRank         | Graph-based ranking (like PageRank)|
| YAKE             | Yet Another Keyword Extractor     |
+------------------+-----------------------------------+

TextRank Graph:
  machine -- learning
     |          |
  algorithms -- NLP
     |          |
  improve -- tasks

Keywords: ["machine learning", "NLP", "algorithms"]
hinglish_explanation: Bhai keyword extraction matlab document se sabse important words/phrases nikalna. TF-IDF se rare important words milte hain, RAKE phrases nikalta hai, TextRank graph banake important nodes dhundhta hai. SEO, summarization, tagging mein bahut useful hai.
real_life_example: IndiaMART products ko automatically keywords assign karta hai descriptions se. Medium India blog posts ke tags automatically extract hote hain content se. Naukri.com job descriptions se skills extract karta hai keyword extraction se - 'Python', 'SQL', 'Machine Learning'.
how_to_answer: - Keyword extraction identifies the most important words/phrases in a document
- Statistical methods: TF-IDF, word frequency analysis
- Graph-based: TextRank builds word graph and ranks by importance
- RAKE: uses word frequency and co-occurrence to score phrases
- ML-based: trained extractors using labeled keyword datasets
- Applications: SEO, auto-tagging, document indexing, summarization
- Libraries: YAKE, KeyBERT (BERT-based), gensim keywords, spaCy

question: What is the difference between multi-class and multi-label text classification?
diagram:
Multi-Class (Mutually Exclusive):
Document -> ONE label only
"Cricket match today" -> Sports (not Politics, not Entertainment)
Softmax output: [0.9, 0.05, 0.05]  (sums to 1)

Multi-Label (Non-Exclusive):
Document -> MULTIPLE labels possible
"Virat Kohli's new brand deal" -> [Sports ✓, Business ✓, Entertainment ✓]
Sigmoid output: [0.8, 0.7, 0.6]  (each independent)
hinglish_explanation: Yaar multi-class mein ek document ko sirf ek category milti hai - sports ya politics ya entertainment, ek hi. Multi-label mein ek document ko multiple categories mil sakti hain - ek article sports bhi ho sakta hai aur business bhi simultaneously.
real_life_example: NDTV news classification multi-class hai - ek article ek hi section mein jaata hai. Par Flipkart product tagging multi-label hai - ek shirt 'casual', 'cotton', 'summer', 'office wear' sab ho sakti hai simultaneously. BookMyShow movies ko multiple genres assign karta hai.
how_to_answer: - Multi-class: each instance belongs to exactly one class (mutually exclusive)
- Multi-label: each instance can belong to multiple classes simultaneously
- Multi-class uses softmax (outputs sum to 1), multi-label uses sigmoid (independent)
- Multi-class loss: categorical cross-entropy, Multi-label: binary cross-entropy
- Multi-class metrics: accuracy, macro/micro F1; Multi-label: hamming loss, subset accuracy
- Multi-label approaches: Binary Relevance, Classifier Chains, neural with sigmoid
- Real-world text is often multi-label (movie genres, product tags, article topics)

question: What are embedding dimensions and how do you choose the right size?
diagram:
Embedding Dimensions Comparison:
+--------+------------------+------------------+
| Dim    | Pros             | Cons             |
+--------+------------------+------------------+
| 50     | Fast, less RAM   | Less expressive  |
| 100    | Good balance     | -                |
| 200    | Rich features    | Moderate cost    |
| 300    | Very expressive  | Slower, more RAM |
| 768    | BERT default     | Heavy compute    |
+--------+------------------+------------------+

Rule of thumb: dim ≈ 4th root of vocab size
Vocab 10000 -> dim ≈ 10 (too small, use 50-100)
Vocab 100000 -> dim ≈ 18 (use 100-300)
hinglish_explanation: Bhai embedding dimension matlab har word ko kitne numbers se represent karna hai. Zyada dimensions = zyada information capture par zyada compute bhi. Kam dimensions = fast par less expressive. Generally 100-300 achha balance hai. BERT 768 use karta hai kyunki large model hai.
real_life_example: Ek startup ne Hinglish chatbot banaya 50-dim embeddings se - fast tha par accuracy kam thi. 200-dim pe shift kiya to accuracy badhi par latency bhi badhi. Production mein trade-off karna padta hai - Zomato ka chatbot 128-dim use karta hai speed ke liye.
how_to_answer: - Embedding dimension = number of features representing each word
- Higher dims capture more semantic info but need more data and compute
- Common choices: 50 (lightweight), 100-300 (standard), 768+ (transformers)
- Depends on: vocab size, corpus size, task complexity, compute budget
- Rule of thumb: start with 100-300, increase if underfitting
- Pre-trained embeddings fix the dimension (GloVe: 50/100/200/300)
- For production: consider latency vs accuracy trade-off

question: What is text segmentation and sentence boundary detection?
diagram:
Text Segmentation Levels:
+-------------------------------------------+
| Document Segmentation                      |
|   "Chapter 1... Chapter 2..."             |
+-------------------------------------------+
| Paragraph Segmentation                     |
|   Split by double newlines                 |
+-------------------------------------------+
| Sentence Segmentation                      |
|   "Hello. How are you?" -> 2 sentences    |
+-------------------------------------------+
| Word Segmentation                          |
|   "Hello" "How" "are" "you"              |
+-------------------------------------------+

Challenges:
"Dr. Smith lives at 42 St. Mary's Ave."
-> 1 sentence (not 3!)
"U.S.A. is a country. It is big."
-> 2 sentences
hinglish_explanation: Yaar sentence boundary detection matlab text mein sentence kahan khatam hota hai ye identify karna. Simple lagta hai par 'Dr.' ke baad sentence khatam nahi hota, 'U.S.A.' ke period bhi sentence end nahi hain. Numbers mein decimal point bhi confuse karta hai.
real_life_example: Legal documents mein (Indian court judgments) sentence boundary detection tricky hai kyunki sections references hote hain - 'Sec. 420 IPC'. Medical prescriptions mein 'Dr. Sharma prescribed 2.5 mg' - yahan dots sentence end nahi hain. NLP tools ko ye sab handle karna padta hai.
how_to_answer: - Sentence segmentation splits text into individual sentences
- Challenges: abbreviations (Dr., Mr., U.S.), decimals (3.14), ellipsis (...)
- Rule-based: use punctuation + capitalization heuristics
- ML-based: treat as binary classification (is this period a sentence boundary?)
- Tools: NLTK punkt tokenizer (trained), spaCy sentencizer
- Important for: translation, summarization, sentiment (sentence-level)
- Language-specific: Chinese/Japanese don't use spaces for word segmentation

question: What is the Zipf's law and what does it tell us about word frequency in text?
hinglish_explanation: Bhai Zipf's law kehta hai ki sabse common word roughly 2x frequent hoga second most common se, 3x frequent third most common se. Matlab bahut kam words bahut zyada baar aate hain, aur bahut saare words bahut kam baar aate hain. Long tail distribution hai ye.
real_life_example: Hindi Wikipedia mein 'है', 'के', 'में' bahut frequent hain (top ranks), jabki specialized words jaise 'अभिकलन' (computing) bahut rare hain. Ye pattern har language mein dikhta hai. Swiggy reviews mein 'good', 'food', 'delivery' dominate karte hain frequency mein.
how_to_answer: - Zipf's law: word frequency is inversely proportional to its rank
- Most frequent word appears ~2x as often as 2nd most frequent
- Implication: few words are very common, many words are very rare
- Explains why stop words dominate and why BoW vectors are sparse
- Motivates: stop word removal, TF-IDF weighting, subword tokenization
- Applies across all natural languages and even programming languages
- Useful for vocabulary size decisions and corpus analysis

question: What is the BM25 algorithm and how is it used for document retrieval?
diagram:
BM25 Score Formula:
score(D,Q) = Σ IDF(qi) * (f(qi,D) * (k1+1)) / (f(qi,D) + k1*(1-b+b*|D|/avgdl))

Where:
- f(qi,D) = term frequency in document D
- |D| = document length
- avgdl = average document length
- k1 = term frequency saturation (typically 1.2-2.0)
- b = length normalization (typically 0.75)

BM25 vs TF-IDF:
TF-IDF: linear TF growth
BM25:   TF saturates (diminishing returns)

TF |          TF-IDF
   |        /
   |      / ---- BM25 (saturates)
   |    /--
   |  /
   +---------> Raw Term Frequency
hinglish_explanation: Yaar BM25 TF-IDF ka improved version hai document search ke liye. TF-IDF mein agar word 100 baar aaye to score bahut high ho jaata hai, par BM25 mein saturation hai - ek point ke baad zyada frequency se score nahi badhta. Plus document length normalization bhi hai.
real_life_example: Elasticsearch (jo Flipkart, Swiggy, Zomato sab use karte hain) default mein BM25 use karta hai search ranking ke liye. Jab tu Flipkart pe 'wireless earbuds' search karta hai, BM25 se relevant products rank hote hain.
how_to_answer: - BM25 (Best Matching 25) is a probabilistic ranking function for document retrieval
- Improvement over TF-IDF: term frequency saturation and document length normalization
- k1 parameter controls TF saturation (how quickly it plateaus)
- b parameter controls length normalization (0=no normalization, 1=full)
- Default in Elasticsearch and Lucene-based search engines
- Works well without training data, pure statistical method
- Still competitive baseline even compared to neural retrieval methods

question: What is the purpose of padding and truncation in NLP models?
diagram:
Batch of sequences (variable length):
Sentence 1: [I, love, NLP]           (length 3)
Sentence 2: [NLP, is, amazing, field] (length 4)
Sentence 3: [Hi]                      (length 1)

After Padding (max_length=4):
Sentence 1: [I, love, NLP, <PAD>]    (padded)
Sentence 2: [NLP, is, amazing, field] (no change)
Sentence 3: [Hi, <PAD>, <PAD>, <PAD>] (padded)

After Truncation (max_length=3):
Sentence 2: [NLP, is, amazing]        (truncated)

Attention Mask (for padding):
Sentence 1: [1, 1, 1, 0]  (ignore PAD in attention)
hinglish_explanation: Bhai neural networks ko fixed size input chahiye par sentences variable length ke hote hain. Padding matlab chhote sentences mein dummy tokens (PAD) add kar do. Truncation matlab bade sentences ko kaat do max length pe. Attention mask se model ko batao ki PAD ko ignore karo.
real_life_example: BERT mein max 512 tokens allowed hain. Agar Flipkart review 600 tokens ka hai to truncate karna padega. Agar 100 tokens ka hai to pad karna padega 512 tak. Production mein batch processing ke liye ye zaroori hai - Swiggy ka sentiment model batches mein process karta hai.
how_to_answer: - Padding: adds special tokens to make all sequences same length in a batch
- Truncation: cuts sequences exceeding maximum allowed length
- Needed because: neural networks require fixed-size tensor inputs in batches
- Padding token has embedding of zeros, masked in attention computation
- Attention mask tells model which tokens are real vs padding
- Strategies: pad to max in batch (dynamic) vs pad to fixed length (static)
- HuggingFace tokenizer handles this: tokenizer(text, padding=True, truncation=True)

question: What is WordNet and how is it used in NLP?
diagram:
WordNet: Lexical Database of English

Synset (Synonym Set):
dog.n.01: {dog, domestic_dog, Canis_familiaris}
  Definition: "a member of the genus Canis"
  
Relationships:
+------------------+---------------------------+
| Hypernym (IS-A)  | dog -> canine -> animal   |
| Hyponym          | animal -> dog, cat, bird  |
| Meronym (PART-OF)| car -> wheel, engine      |
| Holonym (HAS-A)  | wheel -> car              |
| Antonym          | good <-> bad              |
| Synonym          | big = large               |
+------------------+---------------------------+
hinglish_explanation: Yaar WordNet ek bada dictionary/thesaurus hai jo words ke beech relationships store karta hai. Synonyms, antonyms, hypernyms (general category), hyponyms (specific type) sab milte hain. NLP mein word sense disambiguation, similarity calculation, text expansion ke liye use hota hai.
real_life_example: Amazon India search mein agar tu 'sofa' search kare to 'couch', 'settee' bhi dikhata hai - ye WordNet synonyms se possible hai. Educational apps jaise BYJU's mein word relationships sikhane ke liye WordNet structure use hoti hai.
how_to_answer: - WordNet is a large lexical database organizing English words into synonym sets (synsets)
- Each synset contains synonymous words sharing a common meaning
- Provides semantic relationships: hypernymy, hyponymy, meronymy, antonymy
- Used for: WSD, text similarity (Wu-Palmer, Path similarity), query expansion
- Available via NLTK: nltk.corpus.wordnet
- Limitations: English-centric, missing modern words, doesn't cover all domains
- Hindi WordNet also exists (developed at IIT Bombay)

question: What are word analogies and how do word embeddings solve them?
diagram:
Word Analogy: A is to B as C is to ?

king : queen :: man : ?  -> woman
Paris : France :: Tokyo : ? -> Japan
big : bigger :: small : ? -> smaller

Vector Arithmetic:
vec(king) - vec(man) + vec(woman) ≈ vec(queen)

Geometric Interpretation:
        queen
       /    \
      /      \ (gender direction)
    king --- man
      \      /
       \    / (royalty direction)
        woman
hinglish_explanation: Bhai word embeddings mein ek magical property hai - vector arithmetic se analogies solve hoti hain. king - man + woman = queen! Matlab 'king' se 'maleness' hatao aur 'femaleness' add karo to 'queen' mil jaata hai. Ye prove karta hai ki embeddings meaningful relationships capture karti hain.
real_life_example: Ek Indian NLP researcher ne Hindi embeddings mein test kiya: 'Delhi' - 'India' + 'Japan' ≈ 'Tokyo'. Ye property useful hai: agar model ko 'Mumbai:Maharashtra' pata hai to 'Chennai:?' ka answer 'Tamil Nadu' de sakta hai. Educational apps mein analogies test karne ke liye use hota hai.
how_to_answer: - Word analogies test if embeddings capture semantic relationships
- Solved using vector arithmetic: a - b + c ≈ d
- Works because embeddings encode directions for concepts (gender, tense, etc.)
- Classic example: king - man + woman = queen
- Tests various relations: country-capital, singular-plural, verb tense
- Evaluation: find nearest neighbor to computed vector
- Limitations: doesn't always work, biases encoded (man:programmer::woman:homemaker)

question: What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised NLP tasks?
diagram:
Supervised NLP:
+-------------------+     +-------+     +----------+
| Labeled Data      | --> | Train | --> | Predict  |
| (text, label)     |     | Model |     | Labels   |
+-------------------+     +-------+     +----------+
Examples: Sentiment Analysis, NER, Text Classification

Unsupervised NLP:
+-------------------+     +-------+     +----------+
| Unlabeled Data    | --> | Find  | --> | Patterns |
| (text only)       |     | Model |     | /Groups  |
+-------------------+     +-------+     +----------+
Examples: Topic Modeling, Clustering, Word Embeddings
hinglish_explanation: Yaar supervised mein labeled data chahiye - review ke saath positive/negative label. Model seekhta hai label predict karna. Unsupervised mein labels nahi hain - sirf text hai, model patterns dhundta hai khud se. Topic modeling unsupervised hai, sentiment classification supervised hai.
real_life_example: Flipkart ka sentiment classifier supervised hai - purane reviews manually labeled the positive/negative, uspe model train hua. Par Flipkart ka product clustering unsupervised hai - similar products group hote hain bina labels ke. Practo mein doctor specialization auto-clustering unsupervised hai.
how_to_answer: - Supervised: requires labeled training data, learns mapping from input to output
- Unsupervised: no labels needed, discovers patterns/structure in data
- Supervised tasks: classification, NER, sentiment, translation
- Unsupervised tasks: topic modeling, clustering, word embeddings, language modeling
- Semi-supervised: uses small labeled + large unlabeled data
- Self-supervised: creates labels from data itself (masked language modeling)
- Trend: pre-train unsupervised, fine-tune supervised (BERT approach)

question: What are common evaluation metrics for text classification models?
diagram:
Confusion Matrix (Binary):
                  Predicted
                  Pos    Neg
Actual  Pos  [  TP  |  FN  ]
        Neg  [  FP  |  TN  ]

Metrics:
Accuracy  = (TP+TN) / (TP+TN+FP+FN)
Precision = TP / (TP+FP)  -- of predicted positives, how many correct?
Recall    = TP / (TP+FN)  -- of actual positives, how many found?
F1-Score  = 2 * (P*R) / (P+R)  -- harmonic mean

Multi-class averaging:
- Macro: average per-class metrics equally
- Micro: aggregate TP/FP/FN across classes
- Weighted: weight by class support
hinglish_explanation: Bhai accuracy sirf tab achhi metric hai jab classes balanced hain. Imbalanced data mein (jaise spam detection - 95% ham, 5% spam) precision aur recall dekhna padta hai. F1-score dono ka balance hai. Macro-F1 jab sab classes equally important hain, weighted-F1 jab class size matter karta hai.
real_life_example: Flipkart fake review detection mein 99% reviews genuine hain, 1% fake. Accuracy 99% dikha sakti hai bina kuch kiye. Yahan precision important hai (flagged reviews mein kitne actually fake) aur recall (kitne fake reviews pakde gaye). F1-score dekhna padega.
how_to_answer: - Accuracy: overall correct predictions, misleading for imbalanced data
- Precision: exactness - how many predicted positives are actually positive
- Recall: completeness - how many actual positives were found
- F1-Score: harmonic mean of precision and recall, good single metric
- Macro-avg: treats all classes equally, good for class importance parity
- Micro-avg: aggregates globally, biased toward majority class
- Also: ROC-AUC for ranking, Cohen's Kappa for agreement

question: What is data augmentation for text and what techniques are used?
diagram:
Original: "The movie was absolutely fantastic"

Augmentation Techniques:
+-------------------+------------------------------------------+
| Synonym Replace   | "The film was absolutely fantastic"      |
| Random Insert     | "The movie was truly absolutely fantastic"|
| Random Swap       | "The absolutely was movie fantastic"     |
| Random Delete     | "The movie was fantastic"                |
| Back Translation  | EN->HI->EN: "The film was truly great"  |
| Contextual (BERT) | "The movie was completely fantastic"     |
+-------------------+------------------------------------------+
hinglish_explanation: Yaar text augmentation matlab existing text data se naye training examples banana. Synonyms replace karo, words swap karo, back-translate karo (English->Hindi->English). Ye kam data hone pe model ko zyada data dene ka jugaad hai. Low-resource Indian languages ke liye bahut useful hai.
real_life_example: Ek Indian startup Hindi sentiment analysis bana raha tha par sirf 5000 labeled examples the. Back-translation (Hindi->English->Hindi) se 15000 examples bana liye. Quality similar thi. ShareChat bhi regional language content moderation ke liye augmentation use karta hai limited data handle karne ke liye.
how_to_answer: - Text augmentation creates synthetic training data from existing samples
- Synonym replacement: replace words with synonyms (WordNet, embeddings)
- Back-translation: translate to another language and back for paraphrases
- Random operations: insert, swap, delete words randomly
- Contextual augmentation: use BERT/GPT to suggest replacements
- Important for: low-resource languages, imbalanced classes, small datasets
- Libraries: nlpaug, textaugment, EDA (Easy Data Augmentation)

question: What is the difference between a token and a type in NLP?
diagram:
Text: "the cat sat on the mat the cat"

Tokens (every occurrence): 
["the", "cat", "sat", "on", "the", "mat", "the", "cat"]
Token count = 8

Types (unique tokens):
{"the", "cat", "sat", "on", "mat"}
Type count = 5

Type-Token Ratio (TTR) = Types/Tokens = 5/8 = 0.625
(Higher TTR = more lexical diversity)
hinglish_explanation: Bhai token matlab text mein har ek word occurrence. Types matlab unique words. 'The cat the cat' mein 4 tokens hain par 2 types hain ('the' aur 'cat'). Type-Token Ratio se pata chalta hai text kitna diverse hai - higher ratio matlab zyada variety.
real_life_example: Academic papers ka TTR high hota hai (diverse vocabulary), jabki children's books ka low (simple, repeated words). BYJU's content analysis mein ye check hota hai ki class 5 ke content ka vocabulary diversity class 10 se kam ho. Simple concept par important distinction.
how_to_answer: - Token: every individual occurrence of a word in text (including repeats)
- Type: unique vocabulary items (each word counted once)
- Token count >= Type count always
- Type-Token Ratio (TTR): measures lexical diversity of text
- Important for: corpus statistics, vocabulary sizing, complexity analysis
- High TTR indicates diverse vocabulary, low TTR indicates repetition
- Vocabulary size = number of types in a corpus

question: What is negation handling in NLP and why is it challenging?
diagram:
Without Negation Handling:
"The food is good"     -> Positive ✓
"The food is NOT good" -> Positive ✗ (wrong!)

Negation Cues: not, no, never, neither, nobody, nothing, hardly, barely

Negation Scope:
"I do [NOT like the food] but the service was great"
       |--- negation scope ---|

Challenges:
- "Not bad at all" -> Actually positive!
- "No one can deny it's good" -> Positive!
- Double negation: "It's not impossible" -> Possible/Positive
hinglish_explanation: Yaar negation handling NLP mein tricky hai. 'Not good' obviously negative hai par 'not bad' positive hai! 'Nobody can say it's bad' actually praise hai. Simple rule-based negation flip karna kaam nahi karta - context samajhna padta hai. Deep learning models bhi struggle karte hain isme.
real_life_example: Swiggy review 'The biryani was not bad at all' - simple negation detector ise negative mark kar deta hai par actually positive hai. Amazon India reviews mein 'I can't complain about the delivery' positive hai par negation words hain. Ye real production challenge hai.
how_to_answer: - Negation reverses sentiment/meaning: 'good' vs 'not good'
- Challenges: scope of negation, double negation, implicit negation
- Simple approach: negation cue detection + flip sentiment of following words
- Better: identify negation scope (which words are affected)
- 'Not bad' paradox: negation of negative != simple positive
- Deep learning models (BERT) handle negation better through context
- Still an active research area, especially for nuanced cases

question: What is the purpose of an NLP pipeline and what are its stages?
diagram:
NLP Pipeline (spaCy example):
+----------+    +----------+    +-------+    +-----+    +------+
| Tokenizer| -> | POS      | -> | NER   | -> |Dep  | -> |Output|
|          |    | Tagger   |    |       |    |Parse|    |      |
+----------+    +----------+    +-------+    +-----+    +------+

Custom Pipeline:
Raw Text
  -> Data Ingestion (read from source)
  -> Text Cleaning (HTML, special chars)
  -> Preprocessing (tokenize, normalize)
  -> Feature Extraction (embeddings, TF-IDF)
  -> Model Inference (classify, extract)
  -> Post-processing (format output)
  -> Application Layer
hinglish_explanation: Bhai NLP pipeline matlab ek sequence of steps jo raw text se final output tak le jaata hai. Jaise factory mein assembly line hoti hai - ek ke baad ek step lagta hai. Pehle clean karo, phir tokenize karo, phir features nikalo, phir model lagao. Organized aur reproducible approach hai ye.
real_life_example: Zomato ka review processing pipeline: raw review aata hai -> HTML clean hota hai -> tokenize hota hai -> sentiment model se positive/negative predict hota hai -> database mein store hota hai. Har step modular hai - ek step change karo baaki same rehte hain.
how_to_answer: - NLP pipeline is a series of processing steps applied sequentially to text
- Standard stages: ingestion, cleaning, tokenization, feature extraction, modeling
- Pipeline makes processing modular, testable, and reproducible
- Libraries: spaCy (built-in pipeline), sklearn Pipeline, custom pipelines
- Each stage can be swapped/upgraded independently
- Production considerations: error handling, logging, monitoring at each stage
- Tools: Apache Airflow, Luigi for orchestrating complex NLP pipelines

question: What is the difference between precision-oriented and recall-oriented NLP systems?
diagram:
Precision-Oriented (Conservative):
- Returns fewer results but highly accurate
- Minimizes False Positives
- Example: Legal document search (wrong doc = costly)

Recall-Oriented (Liberal):
- Returns more results, catches everything
- Minimizes False Negatives  
- Example: Medical diagnosis NLP (missing disease = dangerous)

Trade-off curve:
Precision |*
          | *
          |  *
          |    *
          |      *
          |         *
          +-------------> Recall
hinglish_explanation: Yaar precision-oriented matlab jo results do wo correct hone chahiye chahe kam ho. Recall-oriented matlab saare relevant results dhundho chahe kuch galat bhi aa jaaye. Medical NLP mein recall zyada important hai (koi disease miss mat karo), spam filter mein precision (genuine email spam mat mark karo).
real_life_example: Practo ka symptom checker recall-oriented hai - possible diseases miss nahi karni chahiye. Par Paytm ka fraud detection precision-oriented hai - genuine transactions block nahi hone chahiye. Trade-off samajhna zaroori hai based on business impact.
how_to_answer: - Precision-oriented: minimize false positives, accept lower recall
- Recall-oriented: minimize false negatives, accept lower precision
- Choice depends on cost of errors in the application
- High precision needed: spam filtering, content moderation, legal search
- High recall needed: medical NER, security threat detection, compliance
- F-beta score: F2 weights recall higher, F0.5 weights precision higher
- Threshold tuning on classifier probability adjusts precision-recall balance

question: What is morphological analysis in NLP?
diagram:
Morphological Analysis: Study of word structure

Word: "unhappiness"
  un-    : prefix (negation)
  happy  : root/stem
  -ness  : suffix (noun-forming)

Morphemes:
+--------+----------------------------+
| Free   | Can stand alone (happy)    |
| Bound  | Must attach (un-, -ness)   |
+--------+----------------------------+

Hindi Example:
"लड़कियों" (ladkiyon)
  लड़की  : root (girl)
  -यों   : suffix (plural + oblique)
hinglish_explanation: Bhai morphological analysis matlab word ke internal structure ko samajhna - prefix, root, suffix kya hai. 'Unhappiness' mein 'un' prefix hai, 'happy' root hai, 'ness' suffix hai. Hindi mein ye bahut important hai kyunki words bahut change hote hain - 'ladka', 'ladke', 'ladkon', 'ladkiyon' sab ek root se bane hain.
real_life_example: Hindi search engines ke liye morphological analysis zaroori hai - 'kitaab', 'kitaaben', 'kitaabon' sab 'kitaab' se related hain. Google Hindi Search internally morphological analysis karta hai. Duolingo Hindi course bhi morphology use karta hai word forms teach karne ke liye.
how_to_answer: - Morphological analysis studies internal structure of words (morphemes)
- Morphemes: smallest meaningful units (prefix, root, suffix)
- Important for: stemming, lemmatization, understanding word formation
- Crucial for morphologically rich languages: Hindi, Turkish, Finnish
- Types: inflectional (tense, number) and derivational (word class change)
- Tools: Morfessor (unsupervised), language-specific analyzers
- Subword tokenization (BPE) implicitly captures some morphology

question: What are common NLP libraries and frameworks and when to use each?
diagram:

hinglish_explanation: Yaar NLTK learning ke liye best hai - tutorials aur examples sab hain. spaCy production ke liye - fast aur efficient. HuggingFace agar BERT/GPT use karna hai. Gensim topic modeling aur word2vec ke liye. TextBlob quick prototype ke liye. Jo kaam hai uske hisaab se library choose karo.
real_life_example: Indian startups mein spaCy production NER ke liye use hota hai (fast hai). HuggingFace se IndicBERT fine-tune karte hain Hindi tasks pe. College projects mein NLTK se start hota hai. Gensim se customer feedback ka topic modeling karte hain Flipkart jaise companies.
how_to_answer: - NLTK: best for learning, research, comprehensive algorithms
- spaCy: production-grade, fast, pre-trained pipelines, entity recognition
- HuggingFace Transformers: state-of-the-art models, fine-tuning, model hub
- Gensim: unsupervised topic modeling, Word2Vec, document similarity

- Choice depends on: task complexity, speed requirements, team expertise

question: What is the difference between batch processing and real-time NLP inference?
diagram:
Batch Processing:
+--------+     +--------+     +--------+
|1000 docs| -> | NLP    | -> | Results|
| (queued)|    | Model  |    | (later)|
+--------+     +--------+     +--------+
Latency: Minutes/Hours, Throughput: High

Real-Time Processing:
+------+     +--------+     +--------+
|1 doc | -> | NLP    | -> | Result |
|(live)|    | Model  |    | (now!) |
+------+     +--------+     +--------+
Latency: <100ms, Throughput: Lower per request

Hybrid:
Batch: Train models, compute embeddings, index
Real-time: Serve predictions, search, chatbot
hinglish_explanation: Bhai batch processing matlab bahut saare documents ek saath process karo - time lagta hai par efficient hai. Real-time matlab ek request aaye turant response do - jaise chatbot. Batch training ke liye achha hai, real-time serving ke liye. Most systems mein dono chahiye.
real_life_example: Swiggy: Batch mein raat ko saare reviews ka sentiment analysis hota hai (daily report). Real-time mein jab customer chat karta hai to intent immediately detect hota hai. Flipkart: Batch mein product catalog index hota hai, real-time mein search results milte hain.
how_to_answer: - Batch: process large volumes together, optimize for throughput
- Real-time: process individual requests immediately, optimize for latency
- Batch use cases: model training, corpus analysis, report generation
- Real-time use cases: chatbots, autocomplete, live translation
- Batch tools: Spark NLP, Hadoop, scheduled jobs
- Real-time tools: FastAPI, TensorFlow Serving, ONNX Runtime
- Most production systems are hybrid: batch for preparation, real-time for serving

question: What is the role of attention mechanism in NLP at a basic level?
diagram:
Translation: "I love my country India"

Without Attention:
Encoder: [I, love, my, country, India] -> fixed vector -> Decoder

With Attention:
Decoding "India":
  Attention weights: I(0.05) love(0.05) my(0.1) country(0.3) India(0.5)
  Focus on relevant words!

Attention Visualization:
         मैं  अपने  देश  भारत  से  प्यार  करता  हूं
I        [**   .     .    .     .    .      .     . ]
love     [ .   .     .    .     .   **      .     . ]
my       [ .  **     .    .     .    .      .     . ]
country  [ .   .    **    .     .    .      .     . ]
India    [ .   .     .   **     .    .      .     . ]
hinglish_explanation: Yaar attention mechanism matlab model ko batana ki input ke kaunse parts pe zyada focus karna hai. Translation mein jab 'India' translate ho raha hai to model 'India' aur 'country' pe zyada attention dega, 'I' pe kam. Ye fixed-length vector problem solve karta hai - har output word relevant input words pe focus karta hai.
real_life_example: Google Translate Hindi to English mein attention use karta hai. 'Mujhe ghar jaana hai' translate karte waqt 'jaana' pe focus karke 'go' generate karta hai, 'ghar' pe focus karke 'home'. Bina attention ke lambe sentences ki translation quality bahut girti thi.
how_to_answer: - Attention allows model to focus on relevant parts of input for each output
- Solves bottleneck of compressing entire input into single fixed vector
- Computes relevance scores between current output and all input positions
- Higher attention weight = more relevant to current prediction
- Introduced for machine translation, now used everywhere in NLP
- Types: additive (Bahdanau), multiplicative (Luong), self-attention (Transformer)
- Foundation of Transformer architecture (BERT, GPT all use attention)

question: What is text summarization at a basic level and what are its types?
diagram:
Text Summarization Types:

Extractive:
Original: [Sent1] [Sent2] [Sent3] [Sent4] [Sent5]
Summary:  [Sent1] [Sent4]  (select important sentences)

Abstractive:
Original: [Sent1] [Sent2] [Sent3] [Sent4] [Sent5]
Summary:  [New sentence paraphrasing key points]

+------------+------------------+------------------+
|            | Extractive       | Abstractive      |
+------------+------------------+------------------+
| Method     | Select sentences | Generate new text|
| Quality    | Grammatical      | More natural     |
| Difficulty | Easier           | Harder           |
| Faithfulness| High            | Risk of hallucin.|
+------------+------------------+------------------+
hinglish_explanation: Yaar extractive summarization matlab original text se important sentences pick kar lo - copy paste jaisa. Abstractive matlab apne words mein summary likho jaise human karta hai. Extractive easy hai par robotic lagta hai, abstractive natural hai par mushkil hai aur galat info generate ho sakti hai.
real_life_example: InShorts app abstractive summarization use karta hai - news articles ko 60 words mein summarize karta hai apne words mein. Google News India extractive approach use karta hai - article ke key sentences highlight karta hai. DailyHunt bhi regional language news summarize karta hai.
how_to_answer: - Extractive: selects important sentences from original text (no new words)
- Abstractive: generates new summary text, may paraphrase and combine ideas
- Extractive methods: TextRank, LexRank, frequency-based scoring
- Abstractive methods: Seq2Seq, Transformer models (T5, BART, PEGASUS)
- Extractive is simpler and more faithful to source
- Abstractive is more fluent but risks hallucination
- Evaluation: ROUGE scores (overlap with reference summary)

question: What is the difference between open-domain and closed-domain NLP systems?
diagram:
Open-Domain:
+------------------+
| Any topic        |
| General knowledge|
| Wide vocabulary  |
| Examples:        |
| - Google Search  |
| - ChatGPT       |
| - Wikipedia QA   |
+------------------+

Closed-Domain:
+------------------+
| Specific topic   |
| Expert knowledge |
| Limited vocabulary|
| Examples:        |
| - Medical chatbot|
| - Legal NER      |
| - Banking FAQ    |
+------------------+
hinglish_explanation: Bhai open-domain matlab kisi bhi topic pe kaam kare - jaise Google Search kuch bhi search kar sakte ho. Closed-domain matlab specific area - jaise hospital ka chatbot sirf medical queries handle karta hai. Closed-domain easier hai kyunki scope limited hai, par domain expertise chahiye.
real_life_example: Google Assistant open-domain hai - weather, sports, cooking kuch bhi poocho. HDFC Bank ka Eva chatbot closed-domain hai - sirf banking queries. Apollo Hospital ka symptom checker closed-domain medical hai. Production mein closed-domain systems zyada reliable hote hain.
how_to_answer: - Open-domain: handles any topic, requires broad world knowledge
- Closed-domain: restricted to specific area (medical, legal, banking)
- Closed-domain advantages: higher accuracy, controlled vocabulary, easier to build
- Open-domain challenges: ambiguity, vast knowledge needed, harder evaluation
- Most production NLP systems are closed-domain for reliability
- Domain adaptation: adapting open-domain models to specific domains
- Trend: fine-tune large open-domain models for closed-domain tasks

question: What is the concept of a vocabulary size limit and how is it determined?
diagram:
Vocabulary Size Trade-offs:

Small Vocab (10K):
+ Fast training, small model
- Many OOV words, poor coverage

Medium Vocab (30K-50K):
+ Good balance
- Some OOV for rare/domain words

Large Vocab (100K+):
+ High coverage, few OOV
- Slow training, large embedding matrix

Coverage vs Vocab Size:
Coverage% |          ___________
          |        /
          |      /
          |    /
          |  /
          |/
          +--------------------> Vocab Size
     (Diminishing returns after ~50K for English)
hinglish_explanation: Yaar vocab size matlab model kitne unique words jaanta hai. Chhota vocab = fast par bahut OOV. Bada vocab = slow par sab cover. English ke liye 30-50K words se ~95% text cover ho jaata hai. Subword tokenization se small vocab (32K) mein bhi 99%+ coverage milti hai.
real_life_example: BERT ka vocab size 30,522 hai (WordPiece tokens). GPT-2 ka 50,257 hai (BPE tokens). Hindi models ke liye IndicBERT ne 128K vocab rakha kyunki multiple Indian languages cover karni thi. Production mein vocab size model size aur speed directly affect karta hai.
how_to_answer: - Vocabulary size = total unique tokens the model can recognize
- Trade-off: coverage vs computational cost and model size
- Larger vocab: better coverage but larger embedding matrix (vocab_size x dim)
- Methods to limit: frequency threshold, top-K words, subword tokenization
- Subword approach: 30-50K subword tokens cover almost all text
- English: 30K covers ~95% of text, Hindi may need larger due to morphology
- Modern models: BERT 30K, GPT-2 50K, multilingual models 100K+

question: What is VADER and how does it perform sentiment analysis?
diagram:
VADER (Valence Aware Dictionary and sEntiment Reasoner)

Input: "The food was AMAZINGLY good!!! :)"

VADER Processing:
1. Lexicon lookup: "good" -> +0.7, "amazingly" -> booster
2. Capitalization: ALL CAPS -> +intensity
3. Punctuation: "!!!" -> +intensity  
4. Emoticons: ":)" -> +positive
5. Degree modifiers: "amazingly" boosts next word

Output Scores:
{'pos': 0.75, 'neg': 0.0, 'neu': 0.25, 'compound': 0.92}

Compound score: -1 (most negative) to +1 (most positive)
hinglish_explanation: Bhai VADER ek rule-based sentiment analyzer hai jo social media text ke liye designed hai. Ye ek lexicon (word-score dictionary) use karta hai plus rules for capitalization, punctuation, emoticons, degree modifiers. Bina training ke kaam karta hai, fast hai, aur social media text pe surprisingly achha perform karta hai.
real_life_example: Twitter India sentiment analysis ke liye VADER quick baseline hai. #ModiSarkar tweets ka sentiment VADER se quickly nikala ja sakta hai. Startup jab MVP bana raha hai social media monitoring ka, VADER se start karte hain - no training data needed, instant results.
how_to_answer: - VADER is a rule-based sentiment analysis tool optimized for social media
- Uses a sentiment lexicon with pre-computed valence scores for words
- Handles: capitalization, punctuation emphasis, degree modifiers, emoticons
- No training needed - works out of the box
- Returns: positive, negative, neutral scores + compound score (-1 to +1)
- Best for: social media, short texts, when labeled data unavailable
- Limitations: English only, doesn't understand context/sarcasm deeply

question: What is the Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenization algorithm?
diagram:
BPE Algorithm Steps:

Initial vocabulary: all characters + end-of-word token
Corpus: "low lower lowest"

Step 1: Character split
l o w _, l o w e r _, l o w e s t _

Step 2: Count pairs, merge most frequent
Most frequent pair: (l, o) -> merge to "lo"
lo w _, lo w e r _, lo w e s t _

Step 3: Next most frequent: (lo, w) -> "low"
low _, low e r _, low e s t _

Step 4: (low, e) -> "lowe"
low _, lowe r _, lowe s t _

Final vocab: {l, o, w, e, r, s, t, lo, low, lowe, lower, lowest, ...}
hinglish_explanation: Yaar BPE ek tokenization algorithm hai jo characters se start karke frequently co-occurring pairs ko merge karta jaata hai. 'l'+'o'='lo', 'lo'+'w'='low', etc. Jab tak desired vocab size na aa jaaye tab tak merge karte raho. Ye common words intact rakhta hai aur rare words ko subwords mein todta hai.
real_life_example: GPT models BPE use karte hain. 'Bangalore' ek token hoga (common word) par 'Bangalorian' 'Bangalor'+'ian' mein split hoga. Hindi mein 'नमस्ते' ek token hoga par rare word 'नमस्कारपूर्वक' subwords mein split hoga. Ye OOV problem solve karta hai elegantly.
how_to_answer: - BPE starts with character vocabulary and iteratively merges frequent pairs
- Greedy algorithm: always merge the most frequent adjacent pair
- Continues until desired vocabulary size is reached
- Common words remain as single tokens, rare words split into subwords
- Handles OOV: any word can be broken into known subword units
- Used by: GPT-2/3/4, RoBERTa; variant WordPiece used by BERT
- Libraries: sentencepiece, HuggingFace tokenizers for fast BPE

question: Explain the Word2Vec CBOW architecture in detail including training process.
diagram:
CBOW Architecture:
                    Input Layer        Hidden Layer      Output Layer
Context words:      (one-hot)          (projection)      (softmax)
w(t-2) [V x 1] ----\
                     \
w(t-1) [V x 1] ------+---> Average --> [N x 1] --> W' --> [V x 1] --> P(w_t)
                     /        ^          ^
w(t+1) [V x 1] ----/         |          |
                     /        W [V x N]  W'[N x V]
w(t+2) [V x 1] ----/

V = Vocabulary size
N = Embedding dimension
Window = 2 (2 words each side)

Loss: Cross-entropy between predicted and actual center word
hinglish_explanation: Bhai CBOW mein surrounding words (context) se center word predict karna hai. Architecture: context words ke one-hot vectors -> shared weight matrix se embeddings -> average karo -> output layer se vocabulary pe probability distribution -> cross-entropy loss se train karo. Trained weight matrix hi word embeddings ban jaati hai.
real_life_example: Flipkart ne product descriptions pe CBOW train kiya tha - 'wireless bluetooth earbuds noise' context se 'cancelling' predict karo. Training ke baad 'bluetooth' aur 'wireless' ke embeddings close aa gaye. Ye embeddings phir product recommendation mein use hue.
how_to_answer: - CBOW takes context words as input and predicts the center word
- Architecture: input (one-hot) -> projection (shared weights) -> average -> output (softmax)
- Training: maximize P(center_word | context_words) over corpus
- Embedding matrix W (V x N) transforms one-hot to dense vectors
- Context vectors are averaged (not concatenated) - simpler but loses order
- Faster to train than Skip-gram, better for frequent words
- Optimization: negative sampling or hierarchical softmax for efficiency

question: Explain the Skip-gram model with negative sampling in detail.
diagram:
Skip-gram with Negative Sampling:

Center word: "learning"
Positive context: "machine", "deep", "is", "fun"
Negative samples: "banana", "chair", "elephant" (random words)

Training:
For each (center, context) pair:
  Maximize: sigma(v_context . v_center)     [positive]
  Minimize: sigma(v_negative . v_center)    [negative]

Loss for one pair:
L = -log(sigma(v_c . v_w)) - Σ log(sigma(-v_neg . v_w))

Negative Sampling Distribution:
P(w) = f(w)^0.75 / Σ f(w')^0.75
(Raises frequency to 3/4 power - gives rare words more chance)
hinglish_explanation: Bhai Skip-gram mein center word se context predict karte hain. Par full softmax (vocabulary pe) expensive hai. Negative sampling shortcut hai - sirf kuch random 'negative' words leke binary classification karo: 'Is this word likely in context or not?' 5-20 negative samples kaafi hote hain.
real_life_example: Ek Indian e-commerce company ne product embeddings train kiye Skip-gram se - center product ke saath kaunse products co-purchase hue (positive) vs random products (negative). Training fast ho gayi negative sampling se - full vocab softmax se 100x faster.
how_to_answer: - Skip-gram predicts context words from center word
- Full softmax over vocab is O(V) - too expensive
- Negative sampling: convert to binary classification
- For each positive pair, sample K negative pairs (K=5-20)
- Negative samples drawn with P(w) proportional to f(w)^0.75
- The 3/4 power gives rare words slightly higher sampling probability
- Result: same quality embeddings, much faster training

question: How does FastText handle subword information and what advantages does it provide?
diagram:
FastText: Word = Sum of character n-grams

Word: "where"
Character n-grams (n=3-6):
  <wh, whe, her, ere, re>  (trigrams with boundary markers)
  <whe, wher, here, ere>   (4-grams)
  <wher, where, here>      (5-grams)
  <where>                   (full word)

Vector: v("where") = v(<wh) + v(whe) + v(her) + ... + v(<where>)

OOV Handling:
"whered" (not in vocab)
  n-grams: <wh, whe, her, ere, red, ed>
  v("whered") = sum of known n-gram vectors!
  
Advantage over Word2Vec:
Word2Vec: OOV -> no vector
FastText: OOV -> approximate vector from character n-grams
hinglish_explanation: Yaar FastText har word ko character n-grams mein todta hai aur unke vectors ka sum word vector hota hai. Biggest advantage - OOV words ka bhi vector mil jaata hai! 'Flipkarting' word naya hai par 'Flip', 'kar', 'ting' ke n-grams se approximate vector ban jaata hai. Hindi jaise morphologically rich languages ke liye perfect hai.
real_life_example: Hindi NLP mein FastText bahut powerful hai. 'Khaana', 'khaane', 'khaaye' - sab ke character n-grams overlap karte hain to related vectors milte hain automatically. Facebook ne Hindi FastText pre-trained embeddings release kiye hain jo Indian startups use karte hain.
how_to_answer: - FastText represents words as sum of character n-gram vectors
- Each word broken into character n-grams of size 3-6 plus the word itself
- Word vector = sum of all its constituent n-gram vectors
- Key advantage: can generate vectors for OOV words from n-grams
- Better for morphologically rich languages (shares subword structure)
- Handles typos and informal text better than Word2Vec
- Pre-trained models available for 157 languages including Hindi

question: Explain Doc2Vec (Paragraph Vectors) and its two variants: PV-DM and PV-DBOW.
diagram:
PV-DM (Distributed Memory) - like CBOW + document vector:
+--------+
| Doc ID | ----\
+--------+      \
                 +---> Concatenate/Average --> Predict center word
+--------+      /
|Context | ----/
| words  |
+--------+

PV-DBOW (Distributed Bag of Words) - like Skip-gram for docs:
+--------+
| Doc ID | ----> Predict random words from document
+--------+

During inference (new document):
- Fix word vectors (trained)
- Train only new document vector
- Gradient descent on new doc's vector
hinglish_explanation: Bhai Doc2Vec Word2Vec ka extension hai jo poore document ka single vector banata hai. PV-DM mein document ID + context words se center word predict hota hai. PV-DBOW mein document ID se directly words predict hote hain. Naya document aaye to uska vector seekhte hain word vectors fixed rakh ke.
real_life_example: Naukri.com resume matching mein Doc2Vec use hota hai - har resume ka ek vector, har job description ka ek vector, phir similarity check karo. Practo mein patient case histories ka Doc2Vec vector bana ke similar cases find karte hain doctors ke liye.
how_to_answer: - Doc2Vec extends Word2Vec to generate fixed-length vectors for documents
- PV-DM: document vector + context words predict center word (like CBOW)
- PV-DBOW: document vector predicts random words (like Skip-gram)
- Document vector is unique per document, shared across all its windows
- Inference: for new doc, keep word vectors fixed, learn only doc vector
- PV-DM generally performs better, PV-DBOW is simpler and faster
- Applications: document similarity, clustering, information retrieval

question: Explain Conditional Random Fields (CRF) for sequence labeling in NLP.
diagram:
CRF for NER:

Input:    [Virat]  [Kohli]  [plays]  [for]  [India]
Labels:   [B-PER]  [I-PER]  [O]      [O]    [B-LOC]

CRF Models:
1. Emission scores: P(label | word features)
   P(B-PER | "Virat") = high (capitalized, person-like)
   
2. Transition scores: P(label_t | label_{t-1})
   P(I-PER | B-PER) = high (continuation likely)
   P(B-PER | I-PER) = low (can't start new entity mid-entity)

Score(sequence) = Σ emission(y_t, x_t) + Σ transition(y_t, y_{t-1})
                  t                         t

Decoding: Viterbi algorithm finds best label sequence
hinglish_explanation: Yaar CRF ek sequence labeling model hai jo sirf current word nahi, previous labels bhi consider karta hai. NER mein ye ensure karta hai ki B-PER ke baad I-PER aaye (valid sequence), I-PER ke baad directly B-LOC nahi aana chahiye. Global optimal sequence dhundhta hai, greedy nahi hai.
real_life_example: Indian court judgment NER mein CRF use hota hai - judge names, case numbers, sections identify karne ke liye. SpaCy ka NER internally BiLSTM-CRF use karta hai. IIIT Hyderabad ke Hindi NER system mein bhi CRF layer hai sequence consistency ke liye.
how_to_answer: - CRF is a discriminative sequence model that considers entire label sequence
- Unlike HMM, CRF is discriminative (models P(Y|X) directly)
- Emission features: word-level (shape, prefix, suffix, embedding)
- Transition features: label-to-label dependencies (valid transitions)
- Training: maximize conditional log-likelihood of correct label sequence
- Decoding: Viterbi algorithm finds globally optimal sequence
- Modern: BiLSTM-CRF combines neural features with CRF sequence constraints

question: What is dependency parsing and how does it differ from constituency parsing?
diagram:
Sentence: "The cat sat on the mat"

Dependency Parse:
        sat (ROOT)
       /    \
     cat     on
     |       |
    The     mat
             |
            the

Dependencies:
sat -nsubj-> cat
sat -prep-> on
cat -det-> The
on -pobj-> mat
mat -det-> the

Constituency Parse:
            S
          /   \
        NP      VP
       / \    /   \
     DET  N  V     PP
     The cat sat  / \
                PREP  NP
                on   / \
                   DET  N
                   the  mat
hinglish_explanation: Bhai dependency parsing mein words ke beech relationships (subject, object, modifier) dikhte hain - directed edges hote hain. Constituency parsing mein sentence ka hierarchical structure dikhta hai - noun phrases, verb phrases mein divide hota hai. Dependency zyada direct aur useful hai NLP tasks ke liye.
real_life_example: Google Search Hindi queries parse karta hai dependency parsing se - 'Delhi se Mumbai ki train' mein 'Delhi' source hai aur 'Mumbai' destination. Relation extraction mein dependency path important hai - 'Modi ne bill pass kiya' se (Modi, pass, bill) relation nikalta hai.
how_to_answer: - Dependency parsing: binary relations between words (head-dependent)
- Constituency parsing: hierarchical phrase structure tree (NP, VP, etc.)
- Dependency captures: who did what to whom (functional relationships)
- Constituency captures: phrase groupings and nesting structure
- Dependency is more useful for: relation extraction, SRL, QA
- Methods: transition-based (shift-reduce) and graph-based parsing
- Tools: spaCy (dependency), Stanford Parser (both), stanza

question: What is coreference resolution and why is it important for NLP?
diagram:
Text: "Sachin Tendulkar is a legend. He played for India. 
       The master blaster retired in 2013."

Coreference Clusters:
Cluster 1: [Sachin Tendulkar, He, The master blaster]
  -> All refer to same entity

Before Resolution:
"He played for India" - Who is "He"?

After Resolution:
"Sachin Tendulkar played for India" - Clear!

Types of referring expressions:
- Pronouns: he, she, it, they
- Definite NPs: "the master blaster"
- Proper nouns: "Sachin"
hinglish_explanation: Yaar coreference resolution matlab pata karna ki text mein alag-alag expressions (he, she, the company, it) same entity ko refer kar rahe hain. 'Sachin ne century maari. Usne 200 Test khele.' - yahan 'Sachin' aur 'Usne' same person hain. QA, summarization ke liye critical hai.
real_life_example: News articles mein 'PM Modi addressed the nation. He announced new policies. The Prime Minister also discussed...' - yahan Modi, He, The Prime Minister sab same. Google Knowledge Graph Indian entities ke liye coreference resolution use karta hai information aggregate karne ke liye.
how_to_answer: - Coreference resolution identifies which expressions refer to same entity
- Types: pronouns (he/she), definite descriptions (the CEO), proper nouns
- Important for: QA, summarization, information extraction, dialogue
- Without it: 'He scored 100' is meaningless without knowing who 'He' is
- Approaches: rule-based (Hobbs), ML (mention-pair, mention-ranking), neural (e2e)
- State-of-art: end-to-end neural models (Lee et al.), SpanBERT-based
- Challenges: long-distance references, ambiguous pronouns, world knowledge

question: Explain extractive text summarization techniques like TextRank and LexRank.
diagram:
TextRank Algorithm (Graph-based):

1. Build sentence similarity graph:
   S1 ---0.8--- S2
   |  \        / |
  0.3  0.5  0.7  0.4
   |      \/     |
   S3 ---0.6--- S4

2. Apply PageRank on graph:
   Score(S1) = 0.35
   Score(S2) = 0.30  
   Score(S3) = 0.20
   Score(S4) = 0.15

3. Select top-K sentences:
   Summary = [S1, S2]

Similarity: cosine(TF-IDF(Si), TF-IDF(Sj))
hinglish_explanation: Bhai TextRank PageRank jaisa hai par web pages ki jagah sentences pe kaam karta hai. Har sentence ek node hai, similarity edges hain. Jo sentence sabse zyada similar hai doosre sentences se (well-connected), wo most important hai. Top sentences select karke summary ban jaati hai.
real_life_example: News aggregators jaise Google News India TextRank-style algorithms use karte hain top sentences extract karne ke liye articles se. Indian judiciary SUVAS system court judgments summarize karta hai extractive methods se - important paragraphs select karta hai.
how_to_answer: - TextRank: apply PageRank on sentence similarity graph
- LexRank: similar but uses cosine similarity with IDF weighting
- Steps: sentence tokenize -> build similarity graph -> rank -> select top-K
- Similarity: TF-IDF cosine, or sentence embeddings for better quality
- Advantages: unsupervised, no training needed, works for any domain
- Limitations: redundancy in selected sentences, no coherence guarantee
- Improvements: MMR (Maximal Marginal Relevance) to reduce redundancy

question: What is topic modeling with LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation) and how does it work?
diagram:
LDA Generative Process:

For each document d:
  1. Choose topic distribution θ_d ~ Dirichlet(α)
     e.g., θ = [0.7 Sports, 0.2 Politics, 0.1 Tech]
  
  2. For each word in document:
     a. Choose topic z ~ Multinomial(θ_d)
        z = Sports
     b. Choose word w ~ P(w|z, β)
        w = "cricket" (likely for Sports topic)

Topics discovered (example):
Topic 1 (Sports):  cricket, match, player, team, score
Topic 2 (Politics): election, party, minister, policy, vote
Topic 3 (Tech):    AI, software, startup, digital, app

α controls document-topic sparsity
β controls topic-word sparsity
hinglish_explanation: Yaar LDA assume karta hai ki har document multiple topics ka mixture hai aur har topic words ka mixture hai. Training mein ye un hidden topics ko discover karta hai corpus se. Input sirf documents hain, output topics (word clusters) aur har document ka topic distribution hai. Unsupervised hai completely.
real_life_example: Times of India news articles pe LDA lagao to automatically Sports, Politics, Entertainment, Business topics discover ho jaate hain. Flipkart customer feedback pe LDA se pata chalta hai ki main themes kya hain - delivery, product quality, pricing, packaging. No labeling needed.
how_to_answer: - LDA is a generative probabilistic model for discovering latent topics
- Assumes: each document is mixture of topics, each topic is distribution over words
- Unsupervised: no labeled data needed, discovers topics automatically
- Hyperparameters: K (number of topics), α (doc-topic prior), β (topic-word prior)
- Training: Gibbs sampling or Variational Inference
- Output: topic-word distributions + document-topic distributions
- Libraries: gensim LDA, sklearn LatentDirichletAllocation

question: Explain the Seq2Seq (Sequence-to-Sequence) architecture for NLP tasks.
diagram:
Seq2Seq Architecture:

Encoder:                          Decoder:
[I] [love] [India]               [मैं] [भारत] [से] [प्यार] [करता] [हूं]
 |    |      |                     |     |      |     |       |      |
 v    v      v                     v     v      v     v       v      v
[LSTM]->[LSTM]->[LSTM]     [LSTM]->[LSTM]->[LSTM]->[LSTM]->[LSTM]->[LSTM]
                  |          ^
                  |          |
                  +----------+
                Context Vector (hidden state)

Problems: Fixed-size context vector bottleneck
Solution: Attention mechanism
hinglish_explanation: Bhai Seq2Seq mein ek encoder sequence padhta hai aur ek fixed vector mein compress karta hai, phir decoder us vector se output sequence generate karta hai. Translation, summarization, QA sab mein use hota hai. Problem ye hai ki lambe sentences ka saara info ek vector mein fit nahi hota - isliye attention add kiya gaya.
real_life_example: Google Translate initially Seq2Seq use karta tha Hindi-English translation ke liye. Encoder Hindi sentence padhta, decoder English generate karta. Ola ka voice-to-text system bhi Seq2Seq variant hai - speech sequence input, text sequence output.
how_to_answer: - Seq2Seq maps variable-length input sequence to variable-length output
- Encoder: reads input sequence, compresses into context vector (final hidden state)
- Decoder: generates output sequence one token at a time from context
- Training: teacher forcing (feed ground truth as decoder input)
- Applications: translation, summarization, dialogue, text-to-SQL
- Bottleneck: entire input compressed into single fixed-size vector
- Solution: attention mechanism allows decoder to look at all encoder states

question: How do BLEU, ROUGE, and METEOR metrics evaluate NLP output quality?
diagram:
BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy):
- Measures precision of n-grams in candidate vs reference
- BLEU = BP * exp(Σ w_n * log(p_n))
- Used for: Machine Translation

ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation):
- ROUGE-N: n-gram recall between candidate and reference
- ROUGE-L: Longest Common Subsequence
- Used for: Summarization

METEOR:
- Harmonic mean of precision and recall
- Considers synonyms, stemming, paraphrases
- Better correlation with human judgment

Reference: "The cat sat on the mat"
Candidate: "The cat is on the mat"
BLEU-4: 0.52 | ROUGE-1: 0.83 | METEOR: 0.78
hinglish_explanation: Bhai BLEU translation quality check karta hai - candidate mein kitne n-grams reference mein hain (precision). ROUGE summarization ke liye hai - reference ke kitne n-grams candidate mein capture hue (recall). METEOR dono ka balance hai plus synonyms bhi consider karta hai. BLEU strict hai, METEOR lenient.
real_life_example: Google Translate quality Hindi-English ke liye BLEU score report karta hai. InShorts summary quality ROUGE se measure hoti hai. Research papers mein Indian language translation systems BLEU aur METEOR dono report karte hain comprehensive evaluation ke liye.
how_to_answer: - BLEU: precision-based, counts matching n-grams, brevity penalty for short outputs
- ROUGE: recall-based, measures how much of reference is captured
- ROUGE-1 (unigrams), ROUGE-2 (bigrams), ROUGE-L (longest common subsequence)
- METEOR: aligns words using exact, stem, synonym, paraphrase matching
- BLEU best for MT, ROUGE for summarization, METEOR for general
- All compare against human reference(s) - multiple references better
- Limitations: don't capture semantic equivalence, need references

question: How is perplexity calculated and used as an evaluation metric for NLP language models?
diagram:
Perplexity = 2^(-1/N * Σ log2 P(w_i | context))

Intuition:
- If model assigns P=1 to correct word: perplexity = 1 (perfect)
- If model assigns P=1/V to all words: perplexity = V (random)
- Lower perplexity = better model

Example:
Test sentence: "The cat sat on the mat"
Model A: P(cat|The)=0.3, P(sat|The cat)=0.2, ... -> Perplexity = 45
Model B: P(cat|The)=0.5, P(sat|The cat)=0.4, ... -> Perplexity = 20

Model B is better (lower perplexity)

Interpretation: Perplexity ≈ average branching factor
PPL=100 means model is as confused as choosing from 100 equally likely words
hinglish_explanation: Yaar perplexity language model ki confusion measure karta hai - next word predict karte waqt model kitna confused hai. Lower perplexity = model achha predict kar raha hai. PPL=50 matlab model average mein 50 words mein se choose kar raha hai har step pe. GPT-3 ka perplexity bahut low hai compared to simple n-gram models.
real_life_example: Jab IIT teams Hindi language models compare karti hain, perplexity primary metric hai. IndicBERT ka perplexity Hindi text pe ~30 hai jabki simple trigram model ka ~200. Lower perplexity = better Hindi text understanding = better downstream tasks pe performance.
how_to_answer: - Perplexity measures how well a language model predicts test data
- Formula: PPL = exp(-1/N * Σ log P(w_i | context))
- Lower perplexity = model assigns higher probability to actual text = better
- Interpretation: average number of equally likely words model considers
- Used to compare language models on same test set
- Limitations: doesn't directly measure downstream task performance
- Typical values: neural LMs 20-60, n-gram models 100-300

question: Explain the attention mechanism (Bahdanau and Luong) for Seq2Seq models.
diagram:
Bahdanau (Additive) Attention:
  score(s_t, h_i) = v^T * tanh(W_s * s_t + W_h * h_i)
  
  Decoder state s_t attends to all encoder states h_i
  α_i = softmax(score(s_t, h_i))
  context = Σ α_i * h_i

Luong (Multiplicative) Attention:
  score(s_t, h_i) = s_t^T * W * h_i    (general)
  score(s_t, h_i) = s_t^T * h_i         (dot product)

Comparison:
+----------+-------------------+------------------+
|          | Bahdanau          | Luong            |
+----------+-------------------+------------------+
| Score    | Additive (MLP)    | Multiplicative   |
| When     | Before decoder    | After decoder    |
| Speed    | Slower            | Faster           |
+----------+-------------------+------------------+
hinglish_explanation: Bhai attention do main types hain. Bahdanau (additive) mein ek small neural network score calculate karta hai - thoda slow par flexible. Luong (multiplicative) mein simple dot product ya matrix multiplication se score milta hai - fast hai. Dono ka kaam same hai: decoder ko batana ki encoder ke kaunse parts pe focus karo.
real_life_example: Early Google Neural MT system Bahdanau attention use karta tha Hindi-English translation mein. Ab Luong-style dot-product attention Transformer mein evolved ho gaya hai. Concept same hai - 'भारत' generate karte waqt 'India' pe focus karo.
how_to_answer: - Both compute attention weights between decoder state and encoder outputs
- Bahdanau: additive score using learned weight matrices and tanh
- Luong: multiplicative score (dot product or bilinear)
- Bahdanau uses previous decoder state, Luong uses current decoder state
- Attention weights = softmax of scores, context = weighted sum of encoder states
- Luong is simpler and faster, Bahdanau more expressive
- Both solved the fixed context vector bottleneck in vanilla Seq2Seq

question: What is Natural Language Inference (NLI) and how is it formulated?
diagram:
NLI Task:
Given Premise P and Hypothesis H, classify relationship:

+--------------------+------------------------------------------+
| Entailment         | P implies H                              |
| P: "A man is eating"| H: "Someone is having food" -> Entails  |
+--------------------+------------------------------------------+
| Contradiction      | P contradicts H                          |
| P: "A man is eating"| H: "Nobody is eating" -> Contradicts    |
+--------------------+------------------------------------------+
| Neutral            | Neither entails nor contradicts          |
| P: "A man is eating"| H: "A man is eating pizza" -> Neutral   |
+--------------------+------------------------------------------+

Models: Cross-encoder (BERT), Decomposable Attention, ESIM
Datasets: SNLI, MultiNLI, XNLI (multilingual)
hinglish_explanation: Yaar NLI matlab do sentences diye - premise aur hypothesis - aur batana ki hypothesis premise se entail hoti hai, contradict karti hai, ya neutral hai. Ye NLP ka fundamental reasoning task hai. Agar model ye kar sakta hai to wo language samajh raha hai kisi had tak.
real_life_example: Fact-checking mein NLI use hota hai. Premise: 'India won the match by 5 wickets'. Claim: 'India lost the match' -> Contradiction. News verification tools Indian fake news detect karne ke liye NLI models use karte hain. XNLI dataset mein Hindi bhi included hai.
how_to_answer: - NLI determines logical relationship between premise and hypothesis
- Three classes: entailment, contradiction, neutral
- Also called Recognizing Textual Entailment (RTE)
- Key benchmark: SNLI (570K pairs), MultiNLI (433K, multiple genres)
- XNLI provides NLI in 15 languages including Hindi
- Applications: fact verification, QA, document retrieval, zero-shot classification
- BERT fine-tuned on NLI achieves ~90%+ accuracy on standard benchmarks

question: Explain aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) and its components.
diagram:
Review: "The pizza was delicious but delivery was terribly late"

ABSA Output:
+----------+------------+-----------+
| Aspect   | Sentiment  | Opinion   |
+----------+------------+-----------+
| pizza    | Positive   | delicious |
| delivery | Negative   | late      |
+----------+------------+-----------+

ABSA Subtasks:
1. Aspect Term Extraction: [pizza, delivery]
2. Aspect Category Detection: [food, service]  
3. Sentiment Classification per aspect
4. Opinion Term Extraction: [delicious, late]

Overall sentiment: Mixed
Aspect-level: More informative!
hinglish_explanation: Bhai normal sentiment analysis poore review ka ek sentiment deta hai. ABSA specific aspects ka individual sentiment nikalta hai. 'Khana achha tha par service bakwas thi' - overall mixed hai par ABSA batata hai food: positive, service: negative. Ye zyada actionable insight deta hai businesses ko.
real_life_example: Zomato restaurant ratings aspect-wise dikhata hai - food: 4.2, ambience: 3.8, service: 3.5, value: 4.0. Ye ABSA se possible hai. Flipkart mobile reviews mein camera: 4.5, battery: 3.0, display: 4.0 aspect-level sentiment hai. Restaurant/hotel owners specific issues fix kar sakte hain.
how_to_answer: - ABSA identifies sentiment toward specific aspects/features in text
- Subtasks: aspect extraction, category detection, sentiment per aspect
- More informative than document-level sentiment for businesses
- Methods: attention-based models, BERT with aspect-specific layers
- Datasets: SemEval ABSA tasks (restaurant, laptop domains)
- Challenges: implicit aspects, multi-word aspects, conflicting sentiments
- Business value: actionable insights (which feature to improve)

question: What is intent classification and slot filling in task-oriented dialogue systems?
diagram:
User: "Book a flight from Delhi to Mumbai tomorrow morning"

Intent Classification:
  Intent: book_flight (confidence: 0.95)

Slot Filling (Entity Extraction):
+------------------+----------+
| Slot             | Value    |
+------------------+----------+
| source_city      | Delhi    |
| destination_city | Mumbai   |
| date             | tomorrow |
| time_period      | morning  |
+------------------+----------+

Joint Model Architecture:
Input tokens -> Shared Encoder (BERT)
  -> Intent head (classification) -> book_flight
  -> Slot head (token classification) -> B-src, I-src, B-dst, ...
hinglish_explanation: Yaar intent classification matlab user kya karna chahta hai (book flight, check status, cancel). Slot filling matlab important details extract karna (source, destination, date). Dono saath mein kaam karte hain dialogue systems mein. Modern approach: BERT se dono jointly predict karo.
real_life_example: IRCTC chatbot mein 'Delhi se Mumbai ki train kal subah' se intent: train_booking aur slots: source=Delhi, dest=Mumbai, date=tomorrow, time=morning extract hota hai. Ola app mein 'Airport jaana hai 5 baje' se intent: book_ride, slots: destination=airport, time=5pm.
how_to_answer: - Intent classification: identify user's goal/action from utterance
- Slot filling: extract relevant parameters/entities for that intent
- Together they form the NLU component of task-oriented dialogue
- Joint models (BERT-based) handle both simultaneously with shared encoder
